1:
Keil and Delitzsch read the chapter as a hinge. The most important features of the national constitution having been laid down, Moses now glances at the manifold circumstances of civil and family life, and takes up here and in the two chapters following the different ways in which the life of an individual might be endangered — the purpose being to awaken in the people a holy reverence for human life. On that reading the legislation about the cities of refuge is not a mere repetition of what Numbers had given, but an admonition to carry those earlier laws out, framed with an eye to the future extension of the boundaries of the land. Since Moses had already set apart the eastern cities, he speaks here simply of the country west of Jordan that Israel was shortly to take, and supplements the older statute with directions about maintaining the roads. Gill fixes the opening clause on the seven nations of Canaan, whose destruction was of the Lord for their sins, and whose land was the gift of one who had every right to dispose of it to the children of Israel. Henry sets the whole under the precept given to the sons of Noah, that whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed.

Gill notes that the three cities were to be separated out of those Israel had taken and settled, and indeed out of the cities given to the Levites; three had already been ordered beyond Jordan, and these were to stand in the midst of Canaan itself. Wesley presses the phrase: in the midst of the several parts of the land, so that a man might flee speedily from any quarter of it. The road-making is described minutely. On the first of Adar, Gill reports, the magistrates met and proclaimed that the ways be repaired, and especially those leading to the cities of refuge; they were made smooth and plain until there was not a hill or a dale to be seen, and bridges were built over rivers and brooks, that the man who had killed by mistake might not be hindered and overtaken. Every obstruction was cleared, and where two or more ways met, that he might not be at a loss for a moment which to take, the word Refuge was written on posts set up for the purpose. Clarke gives the measure the Jews assign — the roads broad, thirty-two cubits, level, free of impediment, and constantly kept in repair. Wesley asks only that the way be distinguished by evident marks and made plain and convenient, to prevent mistakes and delays.

Calvin states the principle the provision rests on: the will is the sole source and cause of criminality, and therefore where there is no malicious feeling there is no crime. Lest the actually guilty escape under the pretext of inadvertency, a mark of distinction is added — that no hatred should have preceded. The instance is of two friends going out together into a wood, and, without any quarrel or wrangling, the head of the axe slipping from the helve and striking the other. God accordingly commands that the motive be investigated, and shows how: whether any previous animosity or contention had arisen, since it is incredible that anyone should be so wicked as gratuitously to rush into so abominable a sin. But the conjecture has room only in a doubtful matter; where a man stabs his neighbour with a drawn sword, the inquiry is superfluous, the guilty intention being manifest. Henry turns the prepared road into application: Christ is not a refuge at a distance, which we must ascend to heaven or go down to the deep for, but gospel ministers are to show people the way to him, removing prejudices as the messengers removed stumbling-blocks.
4:
Not every slayer might claim protection, Gill insists, but only one whose case stood thus and thus, and the illustration is chosen with care. A wood is a place common to men and the cutting of wood a business any man might do, whereas a private place where a man had no right to be, engaged in what was no business of his, made the case suspicious and left him liable to be taken up if such an accident occurred. The Jewish writers put it that a wood is a public place, open alike to him that hurts and to him that is hurt, both having a right to be there. A courtyard belonging to a master of a house is expressly excepted, since neither party has liberty to enter it. Abba Saul reduces the test to a question: what is hewing wood? It is what a man has a right to do, what is public and common and not peculiar to any. The clause about the avenger, Gill adds, hangs on the earlier command to prepare the way and divide the land into three parts, the arrangement being made against the moment when the next of kin, incensed and determined to avenge, sets out in pursuit.

On the promised enlargement the voices diverge instructively. Gill takes the extension of the coast to mean a border carried as far as Euphrates, as it was in Solomon's day, and reports Jarchi's alternative, the giving of the land of the Kenites, the Kenizzites and the Kadmonites; Wesley says simply, as far as Euphrates. Both notice that the grant is conditional on keeping all these commandments — the moral, ceremonial and judicial statutes Moses was then repeating — and Wesley presses the consequence hard. The Jewish writers themselves own that the condition was not performed, so that the promise of enlarging the coast was not fulfilled and there was no need of three more cities of refuge. Yet God, they say, did not command in vain, for in the days of Messiah the Prince the cities shall be added. They expect this in the letter; Wesley answers that it has in Christ its spiritual accomplishment, the borders of the gospel Israel being enlarged according to the promise, and refuge provided in the Lord our righteousness for all that by faith fly to him. Clarke keeps to the history: three more were in fact found necessary, six cities being appointed in all, three on either side of Jordan. He adds that the heathen had their asyla in imitation of these, the Catholics their privileged altars.

Keil and Delitzsch draw the limit sharply: whatever care was taken by the free cities to prevent the shedding of blood, they were never to be asyla for criminals deserving death, nor to shelter a man who had killed his neighbour out of hatred. Should such a one flee there, the elders of his own town were to fetch him out and deliver him to the avenger. They resist the inference, urged by Riehm after Vater and De Wette, that this transfers to the elders the duty of holding a judicial inquiry and deciding the matter, and so opens a discrepancy with the earlier legislation; the elders are simply commanded to do what devolves on them as magistrates and administrators of local affairs. Gill, following the Targum's "wise men of his city," is readier to see a court there, with power to demand the man's surrender and try whether his case entitled him to the benefit of the city. Both agree on the last clause. The eye that must not pity, Gill notes, is not the avenger's, of whom no compassion was to be expected, but the magistrate's: no favour was to be shown because the man was a citizen, a neighbour, a relation, a friend, or rich.
14:
Henry reads the landmark statute as a hedge God has set about men's rights and properties, a friend to human society and men's civil interest. He finds in it an implicit direction to the first planters of Canaan to fix boundaries by the distribution of the land by lot, since it is God's will that every one should know his own, and then an express law to posterity not to shift what was so fixed, by which a man secretly gets to himself what is his neighbour's. The precept he takes to be moral and still binding, forbidding three things: invading a right by forging, concealing or altering the deeds and writings that are our landmarks, or by shifting hedges and meer-stones; sowing discord and manufacturing lawsuits, by confounding the very things that should decide controversies; and breaking in upon settled government by altering ancient usages without cause, so that the law upholds the honour of prescriptions. Gill puts it more plainly still: to remove the mark is to alienate a man's lands to another's use, and leaves the doer obnoxious to a curse. Ellicott finds the connection with what precedes less than obvious, and suggests a caution against a most certain incentive to hatred and murder; he also denies that "they of old time" carries any idea of antiquity, taking it of the first dividers of the land.

Calvin classes the offence as a species of theft, and reasons from the security of possession: for every man's property to be safe, the marks dividing fields must remain untouched as though sacred. He who fraudulently removes one is already convicted by that act alone, since he thereby disturbs the lawful owner in his quiet possession; and he who pushes his own boundary forward to a neighbour's loss doubles the crime by the deceptive concealment of the theft. Whence, he concludes, not only are those thieves who carry off a neighbour's goods, take his money out of his chest, or pillage his cellars and granaries, but those also who unjustly possess themselves of his land. Clarke supplies the antiquarian setting. Before fences came into extensive use, estates were marked by stones or posts, and one of these was easily lifted and reset, so that the dishonest man enlarged his own ground by contracting his neighbour's. Among the Romans the termini were held very sacred and were at last deified: Numa commanded offerings of broth, cakes and firstfruits to be made to them, Ovid records the sacrifice of a lamb and the sprinkling of its blood, Tibullus their adorning with flowers and garlands, and Juvenal annual oblations. Calmet, he notes, found the digests vague on the penalty, though slaves who moved a mark with evil design were put to death, persons of quality exiled, and others fined or beaten.

On the second statute Keil and Delitzsch observe that a rule earlier laid down for capital crimes is here raised into one of general application: no single witness is to rise against a man, that is, to appear before a court or be accepted as sufficient, but everything is to rest on two or three. The verb, they note, means to stand, and so to acquire legal force; and because two witnesses could not always be produced, and one man's statement could not simply be ignored, Moses refers such accusations to the higher tribunal at the sanctuary. Wesley glosses the same word as established, accepted, owned as sufficient. Gill extends the reach of the rule to any sin whatever, capital or pecuniary, against either table, greater or lesser, the Jews excepting only the case of a woman suspected of adultery and the beheading of the heifer. Henry sees the law as favouring the accused, whose life and honour should not lie at the mercy of one man with a grudge.
16:
The case supposed is a false witness rising against a man in a court of judicature, and the two who then stand together are, in Gill's plain phrase, the man that bears the false witness and the man against whom it is borne. The inquisition laid on the judges he takes strictly: they are to look into the nature and proof of the evidence each brings, and the Targum of Jonathan has them interrogate the witness, by whom these things are said, well — that is, thoroughly examine the testimony given and look carefully into it. Wesley marks the asymmetry that makes the statute work. A single witness, though he speak truth, is not to be accepted for the condemnation of another man; but if that same witness be convicted of falsehood, one conviction is sufficient for his own condemnation.

Keil and Delitzsch fix the venue. To stand before the Lord means before the priests and judges who should be in those days, and that at the place of the sanctuary where the Lord dwelt among his people — not, as Knobel supposed, before the local courts. Those judges were to investigate the case most thoroughly, and if the witness had spoken lies they were to do to him as he thought to do to his brother. The clauses from the "behold" onward they read as parenthetical and circumstantial: and behold, is the witness a false witness, has he spoken a lie against his brother? — then ye shall do thus. The verb rendered "thought" they gloss as meaning generally to meditate evil. The law of retaliation that closes the chapter was to be applied without reserve; and they note from Diodorus Siculus that the same law obtained in Egypt with reference to false accusers.

Calvin asks why such a penalty is needed at all, and answers from the state of men. The fear of God does not so prevail in all that they will voluntarily abstain from the love of slander; political laws are therefore enacted against the ungodly and disobedient, so that those who despise God's judgment may at least be brought before the tribunal of men. He observes that perjury is not here ordained to be tried unless someone accuses, complaining that he has been unjustly injured by false witness — yet reason dictates that where a man has been condemned to death by false witnesses the judges should not hesitate to make official inquiry. Since men are generally disposed to assert their own innocence, God thought it enough to put the case of a complaint lodged and diligently investigated, with retaliation following on proof; from which, Calvin adds, it appears that false witnesses and murderers stand in the same light before God. That the inquiry was to be made by the priests as well as the judges, as if God himself were present, he takes as a demand for unusual diligence, a secret crime not being easily detected without the most anxious care.
19:
The measure of the penalty is exact reciprocity. Gill runs through the possibilities: the same fine or punishment is to be inflicted on the false witness that he thought to bring his brother under, whether a pecuniary mulct, whipping and scourging, the loss of a member or the value of it, or death itself — and if death, then by stoning, strangling, burning, or the sword, according to the case. He notes one qualification from Jarchi. Where the accusation was of adultery against a priest's daughter, whose own sentence would have been burning, the convicted witness was not burnt but strangled. Wesley states the rule without the casuistry: what punishment the law allotted to the accused, had he been convicted, the same shall the false accuser bear.

Clarke finds nothing more equitable or proper than this, that a man who tries to injure another, or to take away his life, should on detection be made to undergo the very evil he intended for his innocent neighbour — and he shows how widely the principle has been felt. Some of the better English laws, he says, were made on this very ground: in the thirty-seventh year of Edward the Third it was ordained that all who make suggestion shall incur the same pain the other should have had if he were attainted, should the suggestions be found evil, and a similar law followed in the next year of that reign. By a law of the Twelve Tables the false witness was thrown down the Tarpeian rock. False witnesses, he concludes, have been execrated by all nations.

The deterrent clause Gill reads simply: those who survive the false witness shall hear of the punishment inflicted on him and fear to commit the like sin, lest they be punished in the same way. The command against pity he again refers to the judges, who are not to spare such a man through favour or affection, but to pronounce a righteous sentence in proportion to the crime and see it executed by the rule of retaliation. Life goes for life where the accused must have lost his life had the falsehood not been discovered; where a member would have been lost, or its price paid, the same penalty falls on the accuser — eye for eye and tooth for tooth meaning, in the received Jewish sense, the price of an eye for an eye. Clarke thinks the operation of such a law must have been very salutary, since a man who prized his own members would naturally avoid injuring another's, and regrets that it is no longer in force to restrain the savage acts that disgrace and injure society. He is careful to distinguish the two spheres: a Christian may always act on the plan of forgiving injuries, and where the public peace and safety are not affected he should do so; but if law made no provision for the safety of the community by enactment against the profligate, civil society would soon be destroyed.
